VOGUE
Component 2 · Section B — Magazines · all four framework areas + contexts

Vogue — July 1965 (the mainstream, historical set text)

The Eduqas close-study product for magazines: British Vogue, July 1965, edited by Beatrix Miller, cover star Sophia Loren. Studied in FULL across Media Language, Representation, Media Industries and Audiences, plus its social, historical and cultural contexts. It is the mainstream / historical half of the pairing — the mirror of the alternative, contemporary The Big Issue. Answer the quick-checks to build your score.

Product & contextThe set text at a glance

  • Title / date: British Vogue, July 1965; editor Beatrix Miller. Cover line: "marvellous mad midsummer... sand swim sun sophia loren".
  • Heritage: American Vogue founded 1892; British edition since 1916 (launched when WW1 disrupted US shipping). Long branded the "fashion bible" and an arbiter of taste — it decides what fashion "is, can be and will be".
  • Why it is set: a mainstream, historical product that lets you analyse how a magazine constructs meaning, targets a wealthy audience, operates as an industry, and reflects the values of its time — then compare with the alternative, contemporary Big Issue.

Social, historical & cultural context — 1965

  • A "tipping point". 1965 sat between post-war austerity and 1960s mass consumerism — Britain was becoming more affluent and aspirational.
  • Second-wave feminism was just beginning. Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963) attacked the 1950s ideal that women should find fulfilment only in "husband, home and children". Yet in 1965 that offer was still very limited and depended on access to money — and therefore a successful man.
  • End of Empire: Britain was in the "involuntary dissolution" of the British Empire (India independent 1947). Ideas of exoticism and imperial "otherness" were still fresh — visible in the magazine's imagery (see Gilroy).

Framework 1 of 4Media Language

The cover — how meaning is constructed

  • Masthead: the iconic Modified Didot serif font (introduced 1955, still used today) — heritage, elegance, authority. Here rendered in green over the image.
  • Central image: a mid-close-up of a star, not the clothes — the focus is celebrity persona and beauty, not fashion detail. Direct mode of address (eye contact) hails the reader.
  • Make-up & styling: heavy accented eyes, high cheekbones, full lips — a look popularised by Elizabeth Taylor's Cleopatra (1963). The Turkish headdress ties to Loren's film Lady L (1965) and signals exoticism.
  • Colour & cover lines: jewelled turquoise dominates; playful alliterative cover line ("marvellous mad midsummer") anchors a summer issue.
  • Contents / layout: serif fonts, restrained cream-and-black palette, columns, a Rayne shoe advert with the royal warrant ("By Appointment") — signifying prestige and a wealthy readership. Semiotically (Barthes) every sign — turban, jewels, warrant — carries connotations of luxury and status.
Exam tip: always move from denotation (what you literally see — turban, jewels, direct gaze) to connotation (luxury, exoticism, aspiration) and then to the ideology it constructs (idealised, commodified femininity). That three-step is Barthes in action.

Framework 2 of 4Representation

Idealised, commodified femininity (the cover)

As Van Zoonen argues, the image of Loren as both "woman" and "star" constructs an ideology of female gender identity that is commodified (it sells) and unrealistic. Her styling offers "to-be-looked-at-ness" (an idea associated with Mulvey's male gaze). As an Italian in a pre-mass-travel Britain she reads as exotic — fitting Gilroy's ideas of post-colonial "otherness" and Western fantasies of the East.

The adverts — the limited roles offered to women

  • Revlon "The applied art of eye-making": the woman as art object (pop-art styling), defined by decorative beauty — reinforcing the idea that women must wear make-up to be beautiful.
  • Cutex "bare essentials": a young, blonde, "naked-among-the-leaves" model channels hippy / free-love culture, but the message ("Are you woman enough to wear them?") makes a woman's worth her desirability — natural beauty as sexual availability rather than liberation.
  • Imperial Leather: a "Madonna & child" composition — woman as adoring nurturer, a throwback to the 1950s ideal. The boy is the centre of attention. Second-wave feminism "had clearly not arrived" in this heritage brand.
  • Lack of diversity: the "ideal woman" is repeatedly young, white and blonde — narrow and exclusionary by today's standards.

The "Picnics" feature — femininity & post-colonial "otherness"

  • Woodland glade: women in pure-white Edwardian dresses, parasols, floppy hats, children — and a fawn as a visual metaphor for femininity: beautiful, vulnerable, at one with nature but needing protection. The lone man is in a business suit — his dress signifies control and status, hers signify decoration.
  • Egyptian riverboat: the Egyptian boatman is a hireling of the white couple — a token representation that frames the "real point of identification": the glamorous white Western couple (Gilroy). The woman signifies aspirational exotic travel and "to-be-looked-at-ness"; the man, half out of shot, "dominates" while attending to "important matters".
  • Overall reading: aspirations were expanding but within the controlled limits of patriarchy — women were encouraged to make a "project" of their looks to attract a providing man. bell hooks: women must fight for political rights for real change — a struggle only faintly visible here.

Framework 3 of 4Media Industries

Ownership: Condé Nast & horizontal integration

  • Vogue is the "highly visible centrepiece" of Condé Nast, a large American media group that also publishes GQ, Glamour and Vanity Fair. Owning many titles in the same market is horizontal integration — spreading risk and sharing resources (contrast Disney's vertical integration on the Black Panther page).
  • Vogue is a fashion institution: it works with the major fashion houses and its presence at Paris/New York shows is essential. The "September issue" sets the tone for the fashion year.
  • Hesmondhalgh — cultural industries are risky, so companies rely on stars, formats and branding. Vogue minimises risk through a heritage brand (est. 1892/1916), celebrity covers and a wealthy, loyal readership.

Funding & "monetising the brand"

  • Funded by advertising aimed at affluent readers (cosmetics, fashion, luxury goods). The magazine's aspirational, consumerist tone is what makes its audience valuable to advertisers.
  • Today the brand is everywhere: documentaries (The September Issue, 2009), satirised in The Devil Wears Prada and Ugly Betty (nodding to US editor Anna Wintour). British Vogue's 2019 "diversity" issue was guest-edited by Meghan Markle with editor Edward Enninful — the brand still generating cultural power and revenue.
  • Industry now (the future-of-magazines context): print is in decline and the ad-funded model is "broken"; survivors rely on paying readers, a unique value proposition ("what do you have that no one else does?") and partnerships. Digital-only shifts (e.g. InStyle) and closures make Vogue's brand equity a real advantage.

Framework 4 of 4Audiences

Who was it for — and how is it targeted?

  • Demographic: affluent ABC1 women — the adverts (couture, cosmetics, royal-warrant shoes, luxury toiletries) reveal the assumed spending power and taste. An educated audience is assumed (literary intertextual quotes, sophisticated copy).
  • Psychographics: the issue targets the "aspirers", "explorers" and "succeeders" of Young & Rubicam's 4Cs map — readers who buy Vogue to signal or achieve status and identity.
  • Uses & Gratifications: aspiration & escapism (exotic travel, glamour), personal identity (models of how to look and live) and information (fashion, beauty, what to buy).
  • Stuart Hall — reception: a 1965 reader likely takes the preferred reading (glamorous, aspirational). A modern reader is far more likely to take a negotiated or oppositional reading, seeing the gender and racial representations as dated and limiting.

Pulling it togetherKey theorists for Vogue

Barthes semiotics — signs/connotation on the cover & adverts. Van Zoonen — commodified, unrealistic femininity. bell hooks — feminism as political struggle. Gilroy — post-colonialism & "otherness" (Loren, the Egyptian boatman). Hall — representation & preferred/oppositional readings. Hesmondhalgh — risky cultural industries, managed by branding. Curran & Seaton — concentration of ownership (Condé Nast) & its effect on variety.
